splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA must be finalized. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for the thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected before the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data even if it increases liability for withdrawing employers.

circuits.name: D.C. Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises fundamental questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the period during which violations can be found and punished.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding, so the term expires as originally set and courts cannot extend punishment without explicit statutory authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: The circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any previously presented claim, in addition to satisfying § 2255(h)'s requirements. If it does not, they need only show newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners under § 2255, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to election administration rules. The resolution affects whether voting procedure challenges must wait until post-election or can be addressed proactively, with significant implications for mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when challenging state election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under Title II of the Civil Rights Act?
splits.description: The circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality and business settings, including questions about liability, available remedies, and burdens of proof. The Supreme Court's grant of certiorari indicates the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on these standards.

positions.label: Narrower standards / limited remedies
positions.summary: Holds that claims of discrimination in places of public accommodation are subject to narrower standards of proof or more limited remedies.

positions.label: Broader standards / expanded remedies
positions.summary: Holds that claims of discrimination in places of public accommodation should be evaluated under broader standards with more robust remedies available to plaintiffs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether lenity should prevail over deference to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions in criminal cases. The Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold the opposite. This split has deepened following Loper Bright's overruling of Chevron, which cast further doubt on deference doctrines in criminal contexts.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over Auer/Kisor deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal sentencing contexts, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive authority.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpretations takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's anti-defendant readings of ambiguous Guidelines provisions to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding the career-offender guideline's 'controlled substance offense' definition to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference. Some circuits defer to the commentary under Stinson, while others find the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, making the commentary an impermissible expansion. The Commission has since amended the guideline text, but the split affects cases under prior versions.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition and is not entitled to deference after Kisor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), the First Step Act's safety-valve provision listing three criminal-history criteria, is conjunctive (requiring all three to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one disqualifies).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This determines whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums and leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule criminalizes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires that the substance underlying the state conviction also be federally controlled. Some circuits hold there is no such requirement because the text refers broadly to state law offenses, while others require federal-state schedule overlap. The split affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-schedule limitation required
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes 'offense under state law' and there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the career-offender guideline, so state convictions for substances not federally controlled still qualify.

positions.label: Federal-schedule overlap required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense only if the substance is also controlled under federal law, applying a categorical approach that requires federal-state schedule overlap.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A). The Eighth Circuit categorically bars such consideration, while other circuits and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement amendment (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) permit it. The Seventh Circuit has held that the Commission exceeded its authority in promulgating this policy statement, deepening the divide.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as part of extraordinary and compelling reasons, particularly under the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement allowing sentence reductions for unusually long sentences due to changes in law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the terms of their imprisonment must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights/Bivens actions.
splits.description: The circuits have a longstanding split on the boundary between habeas corpus and civil rights actions for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions (such as First Step Act earned time credit calculations). Some circuits require habeas for any claim affecting the duration of confinement, while others permit civil actions for conditions-of-confinement claims even when they overlap with duration issues.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive remedy for duration-affecting claims
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for challenges to BOP decisions affecting the fact or duration of confinement, including First Step Act time credit decisions, and civil rights actions are unavailable.

positions.label: Civil rights actions available for some confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or Bivens actions to challenge conditions of confinement even when the relief sought may affect the duration of imprisonment, as habeas and civil rights remedies are not mutually exclusive for all claims.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violations of supervised release conditions upon revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on the permissible purpose of a sentence imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits hold that the purpose of the revocation sentence is to sanction the breach of trust, not to punish the underlying violation conduct.

positions.label: Courts may punish for violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions upon revocation, treating the violation conduct itself as a basis for the sentence.

positions.label: Revocation sanctions breach of trust only
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of a revocation sentence is to sanction the breach of the court's trust inherent in the violation, not to punish the underlying violation conduct, which limits the permissible sentence.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that post-petition appreciation inures to the estate upon conversion, while other circuits and the dissent argue that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects debtors by fixing estate property as of the petition date, excluding subsequent appreciation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a)'s definition of estate property.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) fixes estate property as of the petition date, so post-petition appreciation belongs to the converting debtor, consistent with the statute's purpose of encouraging good-faith Chapter 13 filings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (triggering the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, noting the split is lopsided but acknowledging that at least one circuit applies the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil 30-day deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal 14-day deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises out of and is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether orders denying motions to seal medical records satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirement of being 'effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment.' The D.C. Circuit held such orders are immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order, while other circuits have applied the collateral order doctrine more restrictively to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost without immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying sealing motions are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine, as privacy interests can be adequately vindicated through other means such as protective orders or post-judgment review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
